before: Texture mapping paints a picture onto a polygon. Instead of filling a triangle with one colour, or a smooth blend between its corners, the renderer looks up the colour of every pixel it draws in a small image, the texture. In the early 1990s it was what separated the new 3D games from the old: [*Edge*](/vault/magazines/edge)'s caption for *Ridge Racer* in April 1994 asked readers to "remember the blocky pit crew in Virtua Racing? before: A first-person game has to decide, every frame, which walls hide which. A binary space partitioning (BSP) tree does most of that work before the game runs. It cuts the level into convex pieces and stores the cuts in a tree, so that from any viewpoint the renderer can visit the walls in order of distance by asking one question at each branch: which side of this line am I on? [John Carmack](/vault/people/john-carmack) took the idea from graphics research in 1993, while rescuing the Super Nintendo version of *Wolfenstein 3D*, and rebuilt [*Doom*](/vault/games/doom)'s renderer around it. *Doom* walked its tree from front to back and never drew the same wall or floor pixel twice. [*Quake*](/vault/games/quake) took the tree into three dimensions and added a pre-computed list of what could be seen from where.
